mainEntity.name: Why do I get brain fog after eating?

acceptedAnswer.text: Common drivers include large or high-glycemic meals, blood sugar peaks and drops, insulin resistance, dehydration, poor sleep, stress, and certain medications. Daily disabling fog warrants clinician review.

mainEntity.name: Why am I tired after lunch?

acceptedAnswer.text: Post-lunch sleepiness can be normal after a big meal, but daily crashes may reflect glucose variability, insulin resistance, sleep apnea, anemia, thyroid issues, or depression.

mainEntity.name: What is a post meal crash?

acceptedAnswer.text: A post-meal crash is fatigue, fog, or sleepiness 30–120 minutes after eating, often after high-carb or large lunches.

mainEntity.name: Can insulin resistance cause brain fog?

acceptedAnswer.text: It can contribute. Compensatory high insulin and glycemic swings may pair with fatigue, cravings, and cognitive sluggishness, especially with central weight gain.

mainEntity.name: Is brain fog after eating a sign of diabetes?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not always. It can occur with prediabetes, insulin resistance, or non-diabetic meal patterns. Increased thirst, urination, or weight loss raise urgency for glucose testing.

mainEntity.name: Why am I sleepy after eating carbs?

acceptedAnswer.text: Rapid carbohydrate absorption can spike insulin and shift autonomic balance toward rest-and-digest physiology.

mainEntity.name: Can poor sleep make post-meal fatigue worse?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Sleep debt and sleep apnea lower daytime alertness, so lunch can feel like the tipping point.

mainEntity.name: Does food noise relate to afternoon energy crashes?

acceptedAnswer.text: Often. Intrusive food thoughts can lead to grazing and larger meals, worsening glucose swings.

mainEntity.name: When should I see a doctor for fatigue after eating?

acceptedAnswer.text: See a clinician if symptoms are daily, worsening, paired with weight change or increased thirst/urination, or if you snore and wake unrefreshed.
